rows.description: A child learns to clap and congratulate a friend who won a prize even while feeling disappointed. Managing envy enough to celebrate is a skill; pretending there is no feeling at all is less healthy than naming it privately.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: In many Indian families a child greets elders with namaste or touches their feet, and uses respectful address such as ji or aunty. These gestures signal respect and belonging, and their form varies by family, region and faith.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A school-age child compliments a classmate's goal, drawing or answer, and thanks people for help. Compliments can be sincere or a way to gain favour, so context and reciprocity shape how they are heard.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A child begins to feel with another person and also to feel sorry for them, and learns the difference. Guessing another's feeling from the situation is useful but can be wrong, so asking "Do you want company?" is wiser.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Encouraging a friend before a challenge [Expressing]
rows.description: A school-age child says "You can do it" before a race or test. Encouragement signals belief and care; it helps most when paired with a concrete suggestion and does not deny the friend's nervousness.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A school-age child says "I broke it, I'm sorry" and offers to replace or help fix it. Naming the specific act and offering a remedy is more repairing than a vague "sorry if you were upset".
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A child forgives after a quarrel with "It's okay, let's play". Forgiveness can be real or a way to avoid conflict; it does not mean the hurtful behaviour must be accepted again.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A child describes pain by place, kind and level, perhaps using a scale or drawing. Some children downplay pain to avoid fuss or clinics, so repeated complaints or changed behaviour deserve attention.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A school-age child says "I like this one better" or "I don't want to go", and starts giving reasons. Preferences are valid even when they cannot always be met, and explaining limits respectfully keeps trust.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A school-age child criticises rules or teammates as unfair and reports rule breaking. The concern for fairness is genuine, though it can slide into tale-telling or bossiness and needs guidance on tone.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
